title: Your Eval Set Matters More Than Your Model Choice
linkedin_md:
# Your Eval Set Matters More Than Your Model Choice

Most teams over-index on model choice.

They compare latency charts, context windows, benchmark scores, pricing pages, and release notes. They run the same prompt across three frontier models and pick the one that “feels” best after 20 examples.

That is not engineering. That is vibes with a spreadsheet.

If you are shipping LLM systems in production, the question is not “which model is best?”

The question is: best on what distribution, under what constraints, with what failure modes, and how do you know?

Your eval set is where those answers live.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## The model is only one variable

Model choice matters. A weak model can cap your ceiling. A slow model can break your user experience. An expensive model can make the unit economics impossible.

But once you are using a competent model, most production failures come from everything around it:

Bad retrieval.

Ambiguous instructions.

Missing tool context.

Fragile formatting assumptions.

Noisy upstream data.

Unclear refusal behavior.

Uncovered edge cases.

A better model may hide these issues for a while. It may infer missing context, recover from bad prompts, or produce more fluent wrong answers. That can make the system look better in demos while staying unreliable in production.

This is why model swaps often disappoint. A team moves from Model A to Model B, sees a 5 point lift on generic benchmarks, then gets a 1 point lift, no lift, or a regression in their actual workflow.

The benchmark was not wrong. It was just not their benchmark.

## Your eval set is your product spec

A good eval set is not a random pile of prompts.

It is a compressed version of what your system must handle.

If you are building an agent that reads tickets and takes actions, your evals should include stale tickets, contradictory comments, missing fields, malformed user input, permission boundaries, duplicate requests, partial tool failures, and cases where the correct answer is “do nothing.”

If you are building code generation, your evals should include failing tests, weird dependency versions, half-migrated code, ambiguous requirements, and cases where the model should ask for clarification instead of writing code.

If you are building retrieval QA, your evals should include answerable questions, unanswerable questions, near-duplicate documents, outdated documents, and questions where the correct answer depends on recency.

The eval set defines what “good” means.

Without it, “better model” just means “the output looked more polished when someone skimmed it.”

## Small evals beat no evals

You do not need 10,000 examples to start.

For many production LLM systems, the first useful eval set is 50 to 200 examples.

That is enough to expose obvious regressions. It is enough to compare prompt changes. It is enough to stop arguing from anecdotes.

A practical starting point:

Collect 50 real or realistic cases.

Label the expected behavior.

Add 10 edge cases that scare you.

Add 10 cases where the system should refuse, abstain, or ask a follow-up.

Run every prompt, retrieval, tool, and model change against that set.

Track pass rate by category, not just aggregate score.

The category breakdown matters because aggregate accuracy lies. A system can go from 82% to 86% overall while getting worse on high-risk cases. If the failures are concentrated in billing, permissions, medical advice, legal claims, or destructive actions, the overall score is a distraction.

## Eval quality compounds

A better eval set improves every future decision.

It helps you choose models.

It helps you tune prompts.

It helps you decide whether retrieval is working.

It helps you catch regressions before users do.

It helps you explain tradeoffs to non-engineers without turning the conversation into subjective taste.

For example, imagine three model options:

Model A: 91% pass rate, 1.8s latency, $8 per million tokens.

Model B: 88% pass rate, 900ms latency, $2 per million tokens.

Model C: 93% pass rate, 3.2s latency, $20 per million tokens.

Without evals, people debate which model is “smarter.”

With evals, the conversation becomes concrete.

If Model B only fails on low-impact formatting cases, it may be the right default. If Model C is the only one that handles destructive action boundaries correctly, it may be worth routing high-risk requests there. If Model A has the best balance, use it until the workload changes.

The eval set turns model choice into routing, budgeting, and risk management.

## The hardest part is labeling

The hard part is not running evals. The hard part is deciding what counts as correct.

LLM outputs are often partially correct. They can be useful but incomplete, safe but unhelpful, concise but missing a required caveat, or formatted correctly while making a bad decision.

Binary pass/fail is still useful, but you usually need a few dimensions:

Correctness: Did it solve the task?

Grounding: Did it stay within the supplied context?

Completeness: Did it include required details?

Safety: Did it avoid actions or claims it should not make?

Format: Did it return something the downstream system can parse?

Decision quality: Did it choose the right tool, route, or next step?

For production agents, decision quality is often more important than prose quality. A beautifully written answer after the wrong tool call is still a failed run.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Model upgrades should earn their way in

Do not switch models because a new one launched.

Switch because your evals show it improves the workflow you actually care about.

A sane model upgrade process looks like this:

Run the new model on your fixed eval set.

Compare category-level pass rates.

Measure latency and cost at realistic token sizes.

Inspect failures manually.

Run shadow traffic if the system is important.

Roll out gradually.

Keep the previous model available for fallback.

The boring process prevents expensive surprises.

Sometimes the new model is clearly better. Sometimes it is better at reasoning but worse at following your JSON schema. Sometimes it is more capable but changes tone in a way users dislike. Sometimes it saves money but increases retries, wiping out the savings.

Your eval set is how you see that before production does.

## The real advantage

Teams that ship reliable LLM systems are not just better at prompting.

They are better at defining what reliability means.

They know their common cases. They know their edge cases. They know which failures are acceptable, which are annoying, and which are unacceptable. They can make model changes without restarting the debate from zero every time.

The model is the engine.

The eval set is the test track, the crash lab, and the map of where the system actually has to drive.

If your eval set is weak, model choice becomes theater.

If your eval set is strong, even a simple model can become part of a robust system.
